newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Sweden seen set to say No to EMU at start-analysts.
newsitem.headline: Sweden seen set to say No to EMU at start-analysts.

text.p: Swedish politicians are preparing to announce that the country does not intend to join Europe's Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) at its launch in 1999, economists and analysts say.

The latest hint in that direction came on Wednesday when Finance Minister Erik Asbrink said that an EMU decision must match the public view -- and polls show most Swedes are sceptical about a 1999 link.
"The government cannot have a view which runs counter to public opinion on the EMU issue," Asbrink told reporters after a parliamentary European Affairs committee meeting.
"Overall I have not seen any considerable changes in public opinion in the last six months," he said.
Asbrink added that it would take a few more weeks before his minority Social Democratic government would present its views on EMU membership.

The government has previously said it would voice its opinion by the end of May. A party congress will then vote about a possible link in September and a parliamentary ruling will follow before the end of the year.
"We don't expect a 'yes' for an early link on Sweden's part but not a definite 'no' either, rather a soft no, a wait and see," Tomas Pousette, head of economic research at Nordbanken, told Reuters.

Although a decision to keep Sweden outside EMU in 1999 has to a large extent been factored in by market players, economists expect interest rates to edge higher and the crown to soften somewhat when the official statement is released.
"A lot is already in the interest rate spread to Germany. The wide spread reflects the belief that Sweden will remain outside," Hubert Fromlet, chief economist at Swedbank, said.
"The interesting thing is not how much interest rates will rise if Sweden announces that it won't join in 1999, but how much rates could fall if it joins EMU."
The long bond yield spread to Germany currently stands at 130 basis points.
Pousette said there could be a slight negative reaction on interest rates and the currency, maybe also on the bourse.
Economists expect the government to to calm any adverse market reaction by stressing it will keep a tight grip on fiscal policies and will not tamper with its budget targets.
"It's how the government says that Sweden initially will remain outside that matters, whether it sounds positive to EMU or negative," Pousette said.
"The wording is very important and how it opens the door for a future link."

The government can probably not afford to please the market by announcing a 1999 link as it desperately needs to regain voter support ahead of 1998 general elections, and many Swedes are hostile to both EMU and the European Union (EU).

Although opinion polls have showed people turning slightly more in favour of EMU, a Tuesday survey by pollster Sifo indicated that only 26 percent supported 1999 membership, while 24 percent wanted to join at a later stage and 35 percent dismissed a link. The rest were undecided.
But among the ruling Social Democrats support for EMU is declining, down to 44 percent in May from 47 percent in March, the poll said.
At the same time, opinion polls show voters -- stung by severe cuts in the welfare state to improve shaky state finances -- fleeing the ruling party.

In an April survey by pollster Temo, 31.5 percent of voters preferred the Social Democrats compared to 45.3 percent at the 1994 general elections, while the main foe, the conservative Moderate Party, advanced to 32.0 percent from 22.4 percent.

With a new round of elections coming up, the government needs to get on the good side of voters and it might also need continued support from its informal coalition partner, the Centre Party, which opposes EMU membership.
-- Birgitta Forsberg, Stockholm newsroom +46-8-700-1006
